frase_gancho.texto: Feathered jaguars, serpents, and coyotes in procession: the bestiary of Teotihuacán.

puente_narrativo.texto: When the fire of the year five hundred fifty put an end to Teotihuacán, the valley was left without a capital. Continue to the Toltec Hall: there, stone warriors hold up the roof of a temple, and other animals, jaguars and coyotes, parade once again.

guion_corto.texto: Animals hold an enormous place in the art of Teotihuacán. In its murals and vessels appear jaguars with feathers, Feathered Serpents, birds, coyotes in a row, and seashells, sometimes blended into creatures that do not exist in nature. This piece is part of that bestiary. Look for claws, fangs, feathers, and scales on a single body, and notice the scrolls and drops coming out of the snouts: they are interpreted as song, breath, or water. For the people of Teotihuacán, it is thought, each animal had its own power: the jaguar, that of the earth; the serpent, that of water; the bird, that of the air. Together they formed a map of the world.

guion_largo.texto:
In Teotihuacán, animals are protagonists. They appear in murals, vessels, braziers, and reliefs: jaguars, coyotes, owls, serpents, birds, butterflies, and also blended creatures, such as a jaguar with feathers or a serpent with wings. These beings are called mythological because they do not exist, but for the one who painted them they were real: they gathered several powers of the world into a single body.

Think about what each one meant. The jaguar, a nocturnal hunter, was associated with the night, the earth, and power. The serpent, which glides like water, with rivers and fertility. The bird, with the sky and breath. When the painters combined them, they were not inventing monsters: they were writing ideas with images, a language that anyone could read without needing to learn signs.

Coyotes have a special place. In Atetelco, one of the apartment compounds of Teotihuacán, the walls are painted with coyotes in procession, sometimes with symbols of war, and some people connect them with warriors who dressed as coyotes. Remember the carved bone from Tequixquiac, the one in the hall of the first settlers: the coyote runs through the whole history of Mexico, from prehistory to the name of a poet king, Nezahualcóyotl.

The jaguar comes from even further back. The Olmec had already made it their most important animal, and in the Gulf Coast Hall you will see a jaguar child in the arms of a great figure. In Teotihuacán, the jaguar appears with feathers, drinking, roaring, sometimes with a shell in its mouth. It is the same animal, but the city transformed it into a symbol of its own.

The Feathered Serpent, the one on the facade you began this tour with, is also a mythological animal: reptile and bird at once, earth and sky, water and wind. In Teotihuacán it was a symbol of power and order. Centuries later, the Toltec and the Mexica would call it Quetzalcóatl, and the Maya, Kukulkán. It is one of the threads that traveled the farthest.

Among many peoples of Mexico, people still believe that each person has an animal that accompanies them, their nahual. And in the past, it was believed that certain priests and warriors could transform into animals. We do not know whether it was the same in Teotihuacán, but the blending of person and animal is very common in its art. In the Mexica Hall you will see warriors dressed as eagles and jaguars, and an eagle emerging from a warrior’s helmet.

Notice also what comes out of the snouts: curled scrolls, drops, flowers. It is the same idea you saw in the mural of Tlalocan, where words that blossom come out of the mouths. The animals of Teotihuacán do not just roar or growl: they sing, they speak, they breathe the sacred air. Even the wild beasts are poets.

With these animals the Teotihuacán Hall comes to an end. The city we saw, with its pyramids painted red, its water goddess, its paradise, its old fire god, and its stone faces, burned around the year five hundred fifty and was left almost empty. But its ideas did not die: other peoples gathered them up, changed them, and kept telling them.

texto: Look for claws, fangs, and feathers on a single body
Notice the scrolls coming out of the snouts
Count how many different kinds of animals you can recognize

texto.Material: Fresco painting on stucco and lime mortar
texto.Origin: Teotihuacán, State of Mexico (Avenue of the Dead)

texto.pregunta: Myth: These animals were just decoration.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Each animal had a meaning and a power; combining them was a way of expressing ideas in images, like a language without words.
